core_idea: Abstract every pile to the exponent of 2 dividing it, then classify a position using the minimum such exponent and whether all piles attain it. This valuation-based state compression turns the game into a win/lose/draw classification that can be counted by minimum-exponent layers.
key_observations: A move is available exactly when some pile has positive 2-adic valuation; termination means every valuation is zero.
If every pile has the same positive valuation c, any move makes every valuation c-1.
Choosing a pile with minimum valuation m makes all valuations become m-1 when m is odd, producing a favorable uniform state for the opponent classification.
When m is even and all valuations equal m, every move creates the odd uniform state, so the current player loses.
When m is even but valuations are non-uniform, players can preserve a mixed state indefinitely, so optimal play yields a draw.
Configurations with minimum valuation exactly i can be counted as those with every value divisible by 2^i, minus those with every value divisible by 2^(i+1).
reasoning_patterns: Replace numeric values by the divisibility valuation that determines move behavior.
Identify a minimal statistic whose parity controls the game outcome.
Separate uniform boundary states from mixed states with the same minimum.
Prove draws by finding a maintainable nonterminal invariant.
Count combinatorial objects by exact minimum using nested-set subtraction.
questions: Does the move depend only on a number's divisibility level?
What is the smallest valuation present, and how does a move affect it?
Are uniform and non-uniform states fundamentally different?
Can either player maintain a nonterminal mixed-state invariant forever?
Can I count states with an exact minimum by subtracting two threshold counts?
